name: Rafael Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for joining me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you actually think. To start, what's a normal working day like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on a circuit board line at an electronics plant that makes controllers for e-bikes. The main machines are pick-and-place machines, which grab tiny parts off reels and stick them on the boards, then the boards go through an oven. My job is loading reels, keeping the feeders right and clearing faults when the camera rejects a board. Six months in, and I still get the feeder numbers wrong sometimes.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like how fast it is, thousands of parts a minute, it's hypnotic. I use an AI chatbot every day to look up fault codes and to plan my side thing, fixing up second-hand e-bikes. What wears me out is the clean-room gown and the twelve-hour weekend shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, it's a good tool and not a miracle, which is what I thought anyway. I'd keep using it. I'd probably post that the people panicking and the people hyping were both wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it changes nothing for me. The line already runs mostly by machine, and I'm the person who keeps it fed. I've got a bit over a year of pay in an index fund, so I'm not worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working, ask to train as a line technician, which means setting up the machines for new boards. Grow the e-bike repairs to maybe two bikes a month. Keep investing a fixed amount every payday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly bored by it, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How did a 27-year-old end up with over a year saved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I lived in a shared house with four others for years and never bought a car. I put money into an index fund from my first job at a call centre. It's not exciting, it just added up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any pressure in your life that this picture doesn't fix?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent's high in the city and I'd like my own place one day. And the weekend shifts kill my social life. But that's ordinary stuff.

say: I'd say AI is a **good tool**, not a miracle, as I expected.
I'd post that the **panickers and hypers** were both wrong.
think: Privately, nothing changes; I'm the one who keeps the **line fed**.
A bit over a **year of pay** in an index fund means I'm not worried.
do: Ask to train as a **line technician** who sets up machines for new boards.
Grow the **e-bike repairs** to about two bikes a month.
Keep investing a **fixed amount** every payday.
feel: He feels **calm** and slightly **bored** by this picture.
S0.quote: The line already runs mostly by machine, and I'm the person who keeps it fed.
fieldNote: His savings come from **frugal years** in a shared house and no car.
He already runs an **e-bike repair** side business.
His remaining pressures are **rent** and weekend shifts, both ordinary.

steps.text: Apply to train as a line technician for new board setups
Grow the e-bike repair work to two bikes a month
Keep paying a fixed sum into the index fund each payday

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the best time to be young and curious. At work I'd tell people to start playing with the tools now. I'd post a few how-to videos, like how I use AI to diagnose bike motors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think this is good for me. The line gets smarter cameras and smarter planning, and someone has to set all that up. I'd want to be that person instead of the one loading reels.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Push hard for the technician training, and do an online course on machine programming in the evenings. Turn the e-bike thing into a proper registered business. Keep my fund growing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Actually a bit excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would struggle on your line?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The two older operators who won't touch the new screens. They're brilliant with their hands, but if the setup moves to software, they'll get left on the boring jobs. I'd offer to show them, but they'd probably say no.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a risk you're missing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe that everyone young has the same idea. If the technician jobs fill up because everyone young has the same idea, I'd still have the bikes. That's why the side business matters.

say: I'd say it's the best time to be **young and curious**.
I'd post **how-to videos** on using AI to diagnose e-bike motors.
think: Smarter cameras and planning need someone to **set them up**, and that's good for me.
I'd rather be the **technician** than the one loading reels.
do: Take an evening online course in **machine programming**.
Register the **e-bike repairs** as a proper business.
S1.quote: If the technician jobs fill up because everyone young has the same idea, I'd still have the bikes.
fieldNote: He sees this picture as a clear **opportunity**, not a threat.
He hedges the crowded **technician** route with his side business.
He'd offer to help **older operators** but expects them to refuse.

steps.text: Take an evening course in pick-and-place machine programming
Use AI to diagnose bike motors and film how-to videos
Register the e-bike repair work as a small business
Keep adding to the index fund every month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say get ready, because this is the big one. I'd tell friends to cut debt and learn something physical. I'd probably post a long thread about what to do in the first year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my clever plan dies here. Programming the line is thinking work, so AGI does it in 2028, and the robots that load reels arrive in 2031. Both halves of my job go, just three years apart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stop chasing the technician course, since AGI will write the setups. Move my energy into the e-bike repair business, because fixing a stranger's bent bike in a shed is messy hands-on work. Move some of the fund into tools and a small workshop unit, and keep the factory job until about 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I've got money and ideas, but the ladder I was climbing just vanishes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said robots would follow by 2031. Won't they fix bikes too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Eventually, sure. But a robot that can deal with every brand of cheap e-bike, rusty bolts and all, feels further off than a robot that loads reels in a clean room. Clean rooms are made for robots, and sheds aren't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut back on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Eating out and the gym. I'd probably move back into a shared house to save rent while I build the workshop. Annoying at 27, but fine.

I'd post a long thread about what to do in the **first year**.
think: Programming the line is **thinking work**, so AGI takes it in 2028.
Robots loading reels arrive by **2031**, so both halves of my job go.

feel: He feels **anxious**: money and ideas, but his **ladder** vanishes.
S2.quote: Clean rooms are made for robots, and sheds aren't.
fieldNote: He clearly maps AGI to his **setup** ambitions and robots to his reel loading.
He shifts to **messy hands-on** work that robots will reach later.
Even the most adaptive operator becomes **anxious** when his ladder disappears.

steps.text: Build the e-bike repair work into his main income by 2030
Move part of the index fund into tools and a workshop unit
Cut eating out and the gym membership
Move back into a shared house to save rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is tight but workable. I'd tell people to use the first two years to try things. I'd keep sharing what works for me online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years gives me time to do both. I can get the technician job, earn more for a few years, and build the bike business on the side. When AGI arrives in 2031 I'd switch over to the bikes full time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Do the technician course next year. Grow the bikes to maybe five a month by 2029. Rent a small unit in 2030 and leave the factory before the robots, around 2033.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. There's a plan, but a lot rides on the bikes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the bike business doesn't work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd still have the fund and technician skills. If the bikes fail, I'd go wherever the robots are being installed and help put them in, because someone has to bolt them down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does it bother you that you'd be helping install the robots that replace your mates?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. But if I don't, someone else will, and my mates still lose the job. I'd rather be useful and honest about it.

say: I'd say **five years** is tight but workable.
I'd tell people to use the first **two years** to try things.
think: Five years lets me take the **technician job** and build the bikes on the side.
When AGI arrives in **2031**, I'd switch to bikes full time.
do: Grow the bikes to **five a month** by 2029 and rent a unit in 2030.
Leave the factory around **2033**, before the robots.
feel: He feels **uneasy**, because a lot rides on the bike business.
S3.quote: If the bikes fail, I'd go wherever the robots are being installed and help put them in, because someone has to bolt them down.
fieldNote: With five years he can **stack** both routes: technician pay, then bikes.
His fallback is **installing robots**, which he admits feels uncomfortable.
He is **pragmatic** about displacing others: someone will do it anyway.

steps.text: Do the line technician course next year
Grow bike repairs to five a month and rent a unit in 2030

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a great run-up. I'd encourage everyone at work to pick one new skill a year. Online, I'd be the optimistic one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this is the best of the AGI pictures for me. I'd have ten years to become a senior technician, save a lot, and run the bike business properly. At 40 when the robots come, I'd have options.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get the technician job, then aim for engineer within five years. Turn the bike repairs into a shop with one employee. Keep the fund going and maybe buy a small flat around 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Genuinely hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that could go wrong for you in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Getting comfortable. Ten years is long enough to forget the date, so I'd put a reminder in my phone every new year to check where the robots are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your younger self starting at the plant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my younger self to learn the machine's brain, keep a skill in your hands, and never stop saving. That covers most of the pictures you read out.

say: I'd say **ten years** is a great run-up.
I'd urge colleagues to pick **one new skill** a year.
think: This is the **best** AGI picture for me.
At **40**, when robots arrive, I'd have options and savings.
do: Win the technician job, then aim for **engineer** within five years.
Turn bike repairs into a **shop** with one employee.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough to forget the date, so I'd put a reminder in my phone every new year to check where the robots are.
fieldNote: His only named risk is **complacency** over a long horizon.
He combines **technical**, hands-on and savings strategies.
With a decade, he's **calm** about his own future.

steps.text: Move from operator to line technician, then engineer
Open a small e-bike repair shop with one employee
Buy a small flat around 2030 with part of the fund

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it kills the ladder I'm on before I'm even halfway up it. What would help is cheap business loans and workshop space for people starting hands-on businesses, not just more courses.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what I'd say to the older guys on my line. I'd tell them a robot that never gets tired still can't fix an old e-bike in a shed, and that's worth knowing.

headlineQuote: A robot that never gets tired still can't fix an old e-bike in a shed, and that's worth knowing.
portrait: Rafael is a **27-year-old** circuit board line operator at an e-bike controller plant, six months in.
He has over a **year of pay** in an index fund and runs an e-bike repair side business.
He uses **AI daily** and sees steady change as a chance to become a technician.
AGI by 2028 kills his **ladder**, so he turns to messy hands-on bike work.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it removes his **technician ladder** before he's halfway up.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap **business loans** and workshop space for new hands-on businesses.
